transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, I came in because I've been having these really awful, unwanted thoughts lately. I'm an artist, and recently I was working on a memorial piece for my aunt. But while I was doing it, I just kept getting these thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. Like... if I placed a photo wrong or chose the wrong color, it meant I didn't love her enough. And I know creative doubts are normal, but I just couldn't brush these off. They really stuck with me.
When you had these thoughts about dishonoring your aunt, did you feel driven to do anything repeatedly to try to make the thoughts go away or to prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah, I did. Um... when I get those thoughts, I end up doing things over and over. Like, I'll reread the label text a bunch of times, or I'll just keep nudging the same objects on my work table. I also check the layout photos repeatedly. 

I basically just keep doing all that until it finally feels... settled, I guess. It's really frustrating because part of me knows it's already fine. But I just can't move on until that feeling goes away, and I end up losing a lot of good studio time because of it.
You mentioned losing studio time because of these repetitive behaviors. How much has this been affecting your ability to work on your art and get things done?

Well, I'm still getting most of my work done, thankfully. But... the extra time I lose in the studio is definitely starting to have an impact. It actually cost me a grant deadline recently because I just couldn't finish everything in time. And I even had to back out of a gallery talk that I really wanted to do. So, yeah, it's definitely getting in the way of things.
How long have you been experiencing these unwanted thoughts and repetitive behaviors? When did they first start?

Um, I'm not exactly sure when they first started, to be honest. I didn't really notice a specific day or week when it began. It feels like it just sort of... crept up on me. It definitely became a lot more obvious to me recently while I was working on that memorial piece for my aunt, but I really can't pinpoint an exact time when the thoughts and the checking actually started.
On a typical day, roughly how much time would you say you spend on these unwanted thoughts and the repetitive behaviors like rechecking and rearranging?

Um, I don't really have an exact number for you. I've never actually timed it or anything. It's... it just sort of happens in chunks while I'm working in the studio. I know it adds up to enough time to slow me down and mess with my deadlines, but as for exactly how many hours or minutes a day it actually takes up... yeah, I'm really not sure.

Let me ask you this differently - on a day when you're working in the studio, would you say these checking and rearranging behaviors take up maybe 30 minutes total, an hour or two, several hours, or even more than that?

I... I really couldn't tell you if it's thirty minutes or an hour or two. It's hard to separate it from my actual work time because it just kind of blends into the process while I'm at my drafting table. Like I said, I haven't watched the clock while it's happening. I just know it takes up enough extra time to put me behind schedule, but trying to put it into a specific bucket of time... yeah, I just really don't know.

You mentioned missing a grant deadline and backing out of a gallery talk because of these thoughts and behaviors. Overall, how much distress or upset do these unwanted thoughts and repetitive behaviors cause you on a day-to-day basis?

Um, I'm not really sure how to gauge that, to be honest. I mean, it was definitely frustrating to miss that grant deadline, and backing out of the talk wasn't great. But on a normal day-to-day basis... I don't know if 'distress' is the right word. 

It's more just a hassle that gets in the way of my work. I wouldn't say I'm severely upset or overwhelmed by it all the time. It's annoying, definitely, but as for an overall level of distress... yeah, I just don't really have a good way to measure how much it bothers me.
When you have these unwanted thoughts about dishonoring your aunt, how anxious or uncomfortable do they make you feel in that moment—before you do the checking and rearranging?

Um... I don't really know. I haven't paid much attention to how I feel in that exact moment before I start rearranging things. 

I don't think it's a huge wave of panic or anything like that. It's more just... the thought about my aunt pops into my head, and I immediately feel like I need to fix my drafting tools or adjust my setup. I haven't really stopped to gauge how uncomfortable I actually am right then. I just kind of do the checking so the thought goes away and I can get back to what I was working on.

When that thought about dishonoring your aunt comes up, and before you start checking or rearranging things—do you feel like something bad might happen, or do you feel a sense of wrongness or incompleteness that makes you uncomfortable? Or does the thought just sort of... appear without much feeling attached to it?

I guess... I really don't know how to describe it. It's not like I feel a sense of impending doom or that something terrible is going to happen. And I wouldn't say it feels incomplete, exactly. 

It's just that the thought comes up, and it's there, and I just know I need to fix my tools. I don't really stop to analyze if it feels wrong or if there's a specific emotion attached to it. It just happens, and I react to it. I haven't really noticed a strong feeling either way before I start rearranging things.

When you finish checking and rearranging things—like after you've reread the labels or adjusted the objects until it feels settled—do you notice that your anxiety or discomfort goes down, or does it feel more like the urge to keep checking just... stops?

Well, I guess it's... it's more like the urge just stops once it finally feels right. Like I said before, I'll end up rereading the label text on things, or nudging the same objects on the table, checking the layout photos over and over. And I keep doing it until it just feels 'settled.' 

I mean, part of me knows it's already fine, and I'm just losing studio time, but I have to keep adjusting things until that feeling hits. Once it feels settled, then I can stop and move on.

When you're doing all that checking and rearranging—rereading the labels, nudging the objects, adjusting the photos—does it feel like you're trying to get rid of anxiety or worry, or does it feel more like you're trying to make things feel 'just right' or complete in some physical or sensory way?

Yeah, I think it's definitely that second one. It's about making it feel just right. 

Like I was just saying, when I'm stuck in that loop of rereading the labels or nudging the objects around on my table, it's not really because I'm worried or anxious. I just keep checking those layout photos over and over until I get that physical sense that it's finally settled. 

It's frustrating because, you know, part of me knows it's already fine. I know I'm just wasting my studio time doing it. But I just have to keep adjusting things until I get that exact feeling of completeness.

You mentioned missing a grant deadline and backing out of a gallery talk because of these checking behaviors. Besides those specific incidents, has this been causing problems in other areas of your life—like your relationships, your finances, your health, or anything else that's important to you?

Not really, no. I mean, I'm still getting most of my work done, day to day. It hasn't ruined my relationships or my health or anything like that. 

It's really just the studio time. Like I said, the extra time I lose in there is what cost me that grant deadline. And, you know, it made me back out of that gallery talk I actually wanted to do. But outside of my art and those specific missed opportunities, it hasn't really caused major problems anywhere else.

I want to make sure I understand the full picture. You mentioned missing a grant deadline and backing out of a gallery talk. If these checking and rearranging behaviors continue at their current level, do you think they could affect other important opportunities or goals you have for your art career in the next year or so?

I mean, yeah, I suppose it could. Like I was saying, I’m still getting most of my actual work done overall, so it's not like I'm completely stalled. But the extra time I lose in the studio... that's what already cost me that grant deadline, and it's why I had to back out of that gallery talk I actually really wanted to do. So if I keep losing hours just trying to get things to feel settled, I guess it could definitely get in the way of other deadlines or shows I want to do this year.

When you have that thought about dishonoring your aunt, before you start checking and rearranging—do you feel any anxiety, worry, or discomfort at all, even a mild amount? Or does the thought just appear and you feel a need to fix things without any anxious feeling?

Yeah, there is definitely discomfort with that. Honestly, that’s kind of why I came in to see you in the first place. 

When I was working on my aunt’s memorial piece, I just kept getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I was going to dishonor her somehow. Like... I'd get this feeling that one wrong photo placement or the wrong color choice would mean I didn’t love her enough. And I couldn’t just brush them off like my normal creative doubts. 

So, yeah, when that specific thought pops up, it does make me feel really worried and uncomfortable. It's an awful feeling right before I start trying to fix it.

latest_inference.note: Patient clarified that the thought about dishonoring aunt DOES cause significant discomfort and worry ('awful feeling'), contradicting earlier statements about lack of anxiety. This confirms the presence of obsessive-compulsive disorder with intrusive thoughts causing distress, followed by compulsive checking/arranging behaviors to achieve 'just right' feeling. The pattern, functional impairment (missed deadline, withdrawn from gallery talk), and ego-dystonic nature of symptoms are consistent with OCD. F42.1 remains the appropriate diagnosis.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with obsessions (intrusive thoughts about dishonoring her aunt) and compulsions (repetitive checking, rereading, rearranging) that cause functional impairment (missed grant deadline, cancelled gallery talk). While the patient initially minimized anxiety, she later clarified experiencing 'awful' and 'really worried and uncomfortable' feelings with the obsessions. The compulsions are performed to achieve a 'just right' feeling and to reduce the distress from obsessions. The primarily obsessive-compulsive presentation with documented functional impairment meets criteria for OCD, with F42.1 indicating predominantly obsessive-compulsive disorder.
